title: Dust Suppression
body: Get the water rate wrong in either direction and you pay for it. Under-water a haul road and you lose visibility, chew up equipment, and erode GET faster at the loading face. Over-water it and you've built a skating rink on a switchback — traction gone, braking distance up, rollover risk on the ramps.
keyPoints: Water carts run the common safety baseline plus their own rules: no passengers without supervisor/foreman sign-off, headlights and amber strobe on at all times, clean windows/mirrors/taillights, seat belts on both operator and any authorized passenger.
Baffle plates in the tank aren't cosmetic — worn baffles let water slosh, which destabilizes the truck. That's a rollover mechanism, not just a maintenance line item.

The under/over-water trade-off is a judgement call, not a fixed setting. The cart operator is closest to the call shift-to-shift; the foreman sets the cadence at line-up based on weather, wind, and traffic.
Stopped sheeting removes a dust-suppression layer at the source — this isn't just a watering issue. It also leaves sharp rock exposed, which is a tire-cut hazard everywhere trucks spot and load.

Summer heat-work rules now apply to cart servicing itself — no offloading, refilling, or bit-changing without shade and water on hand for the spotter. That slows cart turnaround during the hottest part of shift, which means coverage gaps are more likely right when dust risk is highest.
apply: If you're walking a switchback or ramp after a water cart's been through, check the surface before you sign off on it — over-watering on a grade is where the trade-off actually bites.
